Mr. Lindqvist's list was taped to the refrigerator, two pages in small, slanted handwriting, and Dev had read the first five lines of it. One scoop of food at seven, one at five. Fresh water. Her pill wrapped in cheese on Tuesday. Two walks a day. The rest of it, a long paragraph about a route, he had skimmed and left for later. Pepper was a beagle. A walk was a walk.

For three days Dev walked her the same way, twice around the block, which took eleven minutes by his phone. Pepper pulled at every corner toward the end of the street, and Dev pulled back. On the fourth evening, at the corner of Harmon and Fifth, a squirrel crossed the sidewalk, Pepper lunged, and Dev was left holding a leash with an empty collar at the end of it.

He ran to the end of the block, calling her name. He checked under the parked cars, then behind the hedges on Fifth, then the whole block again. By the time the streetlights came on, his voice had gone hoarse and his hands were shaking. Mr. Lindqvist was coming home on Sunday. It was Thursday.

He went back to the house for a flashlight, and the list was there on the refrigerator where he had left it. He read the second page standing up.

Pepper and I go down Fifth to the river path. She will want to stop at the bench by the boat ramp, where I sit for a while. Then up Water Street to the bakery, where Mrs. Pham gives her the end of a roll if she sits nicely. Home by the alley behind the church. Forty minutes, more if she meets a friend.

Dev read it twice. Then he took the flashlight and went down Fifth.

The bench by the boat ramp was empty. He kept going, up Water Street, and slowed when his flashlight found the bakery. Pepper was sitting on the step under the awning, very upright, facing the door. The windows were dark. She was sitting nicely, the way she had been taught, for someone who would come in the morning.

Dev knelt and buckled the collar back on, one notch tighter. Then he walked her home by the alley behind the church, the way the list said, and let her stop at every lamppost.

On Friday morning he went down Fifth to the river path, and at the bench by the boat ramp he sat down for a while, because Pepper had sat down first and plainly expected it.

The gate comes down with its two red lights
trading places, and my father shifts
into park and turns the engine off,
because he knows this train. It is the long one.

First the engines, three of them, pushing
a sound ahead of them that comes up
through the floor of the car and into my knees,
and then the cars begin, and I begin to count.

Boxcar, boxcar, a tank car black and round,
a flatcar stacked with lumber, then a line
of hoppers, open at the top, heaped with coal
like buckets someone forgot to bring in.

Each one has a name along its side,
painted or stenciled or half gone under rust:
a railroad from a state I have only seen
as a color on the map at school,

a company whose letters stand for words
I will have to look up, a town
I say out loud to taste it, and my father
says it back to me the right way.

Thirty-one, thirty-two. Someone has painted
a blue fish on a hopper, and someone else,
somewhere else, has painted a name
across the fish, and the train carries both.

My father reads the paper he keeps
folded on the dashboard for this.
He looks up once, when I lose count at sixty
and start again at sixty, as if nothing were lost.

Then the last car, and the quiet behind it,
and the bells keep on a while by themselves.
The gate goes up. My father starts the car.
I sit with ninety-four names in my lap,

and the road goes where it always goes,
to the store, to the school, to our street,
the same three places, and I watch them come
as if each one had a name painted along its side.

Mathieu stared at me. Then he asked whether that meant there would be school. I said I did not know, and it was the first sentence I had ever made up myself in French. All four of us stood there arguing about it until the bell.

The historical society in my town occupies the ground floor of an old bank, and its best room holds three wedding dresses. One is silk, from the 1890s, with a waist so small that visitors laugh when they see it. One is from the 1940s and was made, the label says, from a parachute. The third is from 1962. All three are beautifully kept, and I have looked at them many times. What the society does not have, as far as I can tell, is a single apron.

This is not the society's fault. Museums keep what people give them, and people give what they saved. A wedding dress is worn once, wrapped in tissue, and stored in a cedar chest for fifty years. An apron is worn every day until it wears out, and then it becomes a rag, and then it is gone. Curators of clothing collections often point out that their shelves are crowded with the clothes of special occasions and nearly empty of the clothes of work. The past we can visit is, in large part, the past on its best days.

That would matter less if visitors understood it. Most of them, I suspect, walk past the three dresses and come away believing they have seen how women in this town once dressed. They have seen how a few women dressed for a few hours. The kitchen, the field, and the shop counter, where those same women spent most of their lives, have left almost nothing behind.

The remedy is to collect the ordinary on purpose, and to do it now, while it is still ordinary. A museum could ask for a school lunch menu, a bus transfer, a worn pair of work gloves, a cereal box. Today these things seem too common to keep. That is exactly why they will be rare in fifty years, when no one has kept them.

Some people object that storage is limited, and it is. But a cereal box takes up less room than one wedding dress in its case. The harder objection is that ordinary things are dull. A dress has a story: a bride, a date, a parachute. A pair of gloves seems to have none. But that is only because we already know the gloves' story too well to see it.

In the 1850s nearly every house in Asher's Mill had a clock, and nearly every clock told a different time. Each was set by its owner's best guess and then left to run fast or slow as it pleased. The church sexton rang the noon bell when his own watch said noon, and the schoolmaster, whose watch disagreed, often kept the children ten minutes past it.

Elias Tamm, the town's clockmaker, thought this was a problem a clockmaker ought to solve. In 1856 he set a narrow brass strip into the sill of his shop's south window, placed so that the shadow of the window frame fell exactly along it at the moment the sun stood highest. On every clear day he checked his best clock against that line. The sun is a slightly irregular timekeeper, running some minutes fast or slow depending on the season, so he corrected each reading by a table printed in the almanac. Then he set the clock in the window, a tall case clock with a face the size of a dinner plate, and painted above it in gilt letters: TRUE TIME.

Within a few years the window had become the town's clock. People stopped on their way past to set their watches, and the sexton began ringing the bell by it.

The railroad reached Asher's Mill in 1867, and with it came a second time. The railroad ran its trains by the time kept in Corlett, the company's headquarters, about a hundred miles to the east. Because the sun reaches its highest point earlier the farther east one stands, noon in Corlett came roughly eight minutes before noon in Asher's Mill. The station clock, set by telegraph from Corlett, ran eight minutes ahead of Tamm's window.

The difference caused more trouble than eight minutes should. Travelers who had set their watches by the window reached the depot in time to watch their train pull out. Letters to the newspaper demanded that one clock or the other be changed. The railroad would not alter its time for one small town, and Tamm declined to set TRUE TIME to a noon that was, by the sun, wrong.

His answer, in 1869, was a second clock. He hung it beside the first, set it eight minutes ahead, and lettered above it RAILROAD TIME. It was a neat solution, since it let the town keep both the sun and the trains. The two faces hung side by side for the next fourteen years, and the town learned to read both: TRUE TIME for church and school, RAILROAD TIME for the depot. Visitors thought the arrangement strange. People in Asher's Mill seem to have found it simple.

In November 1883 the railroads of the United States and Canada adopted standard time zones, and the station clock was reset once more. Tamm, by then an old man, reset his second clock to match it and relettered it STANDARD TIME. Within a few years most of the town set its watches by the second clock, and the first was consulted mainly by the old. When Tamm died in 1891, his son took TRUE TIME down from the window.

item.passage:
On a summer night, a bat hunting insects over a field finds its prey largely by sound. As it flies, it gives a steady series of short calls and listens for the echoes that bounce back from anything in its path. Most of these calls are pitched far too high for people to hear. Human hearing tops out at roughly twenty thousand vibrations per second, and many bats call at two or more times that rate.

The echo carries a surprising amount of information. Sound travels through air at about 340 meters per second, so an echo from a moth one meter away returns in about six thousandths of a second, and the delay grows with distance. By timing that delay, a bat can judge how far away the moth is, and differences between what its two ears receive appear to help it judge direction. As the bat closes in, it calls faster and faster, from perhaps ten calls a second while searching to as many as two hundred in the last moments before a catch. Each call, in effect, updates the bat's picture of where its prey has gone. It is a remarkably precise system, and many of the bats that use it weigh less than a slice of bread.

Moths, however, are not simply targets. Many kinds of moths have ears: thin membranes on the body, some with only two sensing cells, tuned to the pitches bats use. Experiments beginning in the 1950s showed what these ears are for. When a moth hears a faint bat call, from a bat still some distance away, it tends to turn and fly away from the sound. When the call is loud, meaning the bat is close, many moths do something more drastic: they fold their wings and drop, or fly in sudden loops and spirals toward the ground. Such simple ears, it seems, save many moths' lives.

Some moths go further. Certain tiger moths answer a bat's approach with rapid clicks of their own. In some species the clicks appear to warn the bat that the moth tastes bad, much as bright colors warn a bird. In at least one species, experiments suggest that the clicks may interfere with the bat's ability to track its target, as though the moth were jamming its signal.

Bats, in turn, have answers of their own. A few species call so quietly that moths hear them only when it is too late to escape, and others call at pitches that many moths hear poorly. Neither side has won. Over a very long time, each appears to have shaped the other, and on any summer night the contest goes on over our heads, almost entirely in a register far above the range of human hearing.

item.prompt: The author's attitude toward the abilities of the bats and moths described is best described as
choices: appreciative
whimsical
apprehensive

item.passage:
On a summer night, a bat hunting insects over a field finds its prey largely by sound. As it flies, it gives a steady series of short calls and listens for the echoes that bounce back from anything in its path. Most of these calls are pitched far too high for people to hear. Human hearing tops out at roughly twenty thousand vibrations per second, and many bats call at two or more times that rate.

The echo carries a surprising amount of information. Sound travels through air at about 340 meters per second, so an echo from a moth one meter away returns in about six thousandths of a second, and the delay grows with distance. By timing that delay, a bat can judge how far away the moth is, and differences between what its two ears receive appear to help it judge direction. As the bat closes in, it calls faster and faster, from perhaps ten calls a second while searching to as many as two hundred in the last moments before a catch. Each call, in effect, updates the bat's picture of where its prey has gone. It is a remarkably precise system, and many of the bats that use it weigh less than a slice of bread.

Moths, however, are not simply targets. Many kinds of moths have ears: thin membranes on the body, some with only two sensing cells, tuned to the pitches bats use. Experiments beginning in the 1950s showed what these ears are for. When a moth hears a faint bat call, from a bat still some distance away, it tends to turn and fly away from the sound. When the call is loud, meaning the bat is close, many moths do something more drastic: they fold their wings and drop, or fly in sudden loops and spirals toward the ground. Such simple ears, it seems, save many moths' lives.

Some moths go further. Certain tiger moths answer a bat's approach with rapid clicks of their own. In some species the clicks appear to warn the bat that the moth tastes bad, much as bright colors warn a bird. In at least one species, experiments suggest that the clicks may interfere with the bat's ability to track its target, as though the moth were jamming its signal.

Bats, in turn, have answers of their own. A few species call so quietly that moths hear them only when it is too late to escape, and others call at pitches that many moths hear poorly. Neither side has won. Over a very long time, each appears to have shaped the other, and on any summer night the contest goes on over our heads, almost entirely in a register far above the range of human hearing.
